Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.\n\nUse active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: \"Save changes,\" not \"Submit.\" An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says \"Publish\" produces a toast that says \"Published.\" The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.\n\nTreat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. \nL233:   * Troubleshoot\nL234: \nL235:   * 【21†Troubleshoot with SSH】\nL236: \nL237: [Button: Send feedback ]\nL238: # Using WebSockets Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences.\nL239: \nL240: This page provides guidance and best practices for running WebSockets or other streaming services on Cloud Run and writing clients for such services.\nL241: WebSockets applications are supported on Cloud Run with no additional configuration required. However, WebSockets streams are HTTP requests, which are still subject to the 【22†request timeout】 configured for your Cloud Run service, so you need to do the following:\nL242:   * Increase the 【22†request timeout】 period to the maximum duration you would like to keep the WebSockets stream open, for example 60 minutes.\nL243:   * Ensure your clients are able to 【23†reconnect】.\nL244:   * Consider using 【24†session affinity】 for clients to reconnect as much as possible to the same instance.\nL245:   * Don't enable 【25†HTTP/2 end-to-end】.\nL246: Though 【24†session affinity】 on Cloud Run provides best effort affinity, new WebSockets requests could still potentially connect to different instances, due to built-in load balancing. To solve this problem, you need to 【26†synchronize data between instances】.\nL247: \nL248: Note that WebSockets on Cloud Run are also supported if you are using 【27†Cloud Load Balancing】.\nL249: ## Deploying a sample WebSockets service\nL250: \nL251: Use Cloud Shell to quickly deploy a sample whiteboard service that uses WebSockets with Cloud Run: 【28†Deploy a sample†deploy.cloud.run】\nL252: \nL253: Or, if you want to deploy that sample whiteboard service manually:\nL254: \nL255:   1. Clone the Socket.IO repository locally using git command-line tool:\nL256: \nL257:     `git clone https://github.com/socketio/socket.io.git\nL258:     `\nL259: \nL260:   2. Navigate into the sample directory:\nL261: \nL262:     `cd socket.io/examples/whiteboard/\nL263:     `\nL264:   3. Deploy a new Cloud Run service by building the service from source code using 【29†the Google Cloud CLI】:\nL265: \nL266:     `gcloud run deploy whiteboard --allow-unauthenticated --source=.\nL267:     `\nL268: \nL269:   4. After the service is deployed, open two separate browser tabs and navigate to the service URL. Anything you draw in one tab should propagate to the other tab (and vice versa) since the clients are connected to the same instance over WebSockets.\nL270: ## WebSockets chat sample full tutorial\nL271: \nL272: If you want a full code walkthrough, additional code samples are available in the topic 【30†Building a WebSocket Chat service for Cloud Run tutorial】.\nL273: \nL274: ## Best Practices\nL275: \nL276: The most difficult part of creating WebSockets services on Cloud Run is synchronizing data between multiple Cloud Run instances. This is difficult because of the autoscaling and stateless nature of instances, and because of the limits for 【31†concurrency】 and 【22†request timeouts】.\nL277: ### Handling request timeouts and client reconnects\nL278: \nL279: WebSockets requests are treated as long-running HTTP requests in Cloud Run. They are subject to 【22†request timeouts】 (currently up to 【32†60 minutes】 and defaults to 5 minutes) even if your application server does not enforce any timeouts.\nL280: \nL281: Accordingly, if the client keeps the connection open longer than the required timeout configured for the Cloud Run service, the client will be disconnected when the request times out.\nL282: Therefore, WebSockets clients connecting to Cloud Run should handle reconnecting to the server if the request times out or the server disconnects. You can achieve this in browser-based clients by using libraries such as 【33†reconnecting-websocket†github.com】 or by handling \"disconnect\" events if you are using the 【34†SocketIO†socket.io】 library.\nL283: ### Billing incurred when using WebSockets\nL284: \nL285: A Cloud Run instance that has any open WebSocket connection is considered active, so CPU is allocated and the service is 【35†billed†cloud.google.com】 as instance-based billing.\nL286: ### Maximizing concurrency\nL287: \nL288: WebSockets services are typically designed to handle many connections simultaneously. Since Cloud Run supports 【31†concurrent connections】 (up to 【32†1,000 per container】), Google recommends that you increase the maximum concurrency setting for your container to a higher value than the default if your service is able to handle the load with given resources.\nL289: ### About sticky sessions (session affinity)\nL290: \nL291: Because WebSockets connections are stateful, the client will stay connected to the same container on Cloud Run throughout the lifespan of the connection. This naturally offers a session stickiness within the context of a single WebSocket connection.\nL292: For multiple and subsequent WebSockets connections, you can configure your Cloud Run service to use 【24†session affinity】, but this provides a best effort affinity, so WebSockets requests could still potentially end up at different instances. Clients connecting to your Cloud Run service might end up being serviced by different instances that do not coordinate or share data.\nL293: To mitigate this, you need to use an external data storage to synchronize state between Cloud Run instances, which is explained in the next section.\nL294: ### Synchronizing data between instances\nL295: \nL296: You need to synchronize data to make sure clients connecting to a Cloud Run service receive the same data from the WebSockets connection.\nL297: \nL298: For example, suppose you are building a chatroom service using WebSockets and set your 【31†maximum concurrency】 setting to `1,000`. If more than `1,000` users connect to this service at the same time, they will be served by different instances, and therefore, they will not be able to see the same messages in the chatroom.\nL299: To synchronize data between your Cloud Run instances, such as receiving the messages posted to a chatroom from on all instances, you need an external data storage system, such as a database or a message queue.\nL300: If you use an external database such as 【36†Cloud SQL†cloud.google.com】, you can send messages to the database and poll from the database periodically. However, note that Cloud Run instances 【37†do not have CPU】 when the container is not handling any requests. If your service primarily handles WebSockets requests, then the container will have CPU allocated as long as there is at least one client connected to it.\nL301: Message queues work better to synchronize data between Cloud Run containers in real-time, because the external message queues cannot address each instance to \"push\" data. Your services need to \"pull\" new messages from the message queue by establishing a connection to the message queue.\nL302: Google recommends that you use external message queue systems such as 【38†Redis Pub/Sub†redis.io】 (【39†Memorystore†cloud.google.com】) or 【40†Firestore real-time updates】 that can deliver updates to all instances over connections initiated by the container instance.\nL303: #### Using Redis Pub/Sub\nL304: \nL305: 【41†Image: WebSockets chatroom service architecture】\nL306: \nL307: You can use the 【38†Redis Pub/Sub mechanism†redis.io】 by creating a Redis instance from 【39†Memorystore†cloud.google.com】. If you are using the Socket.IO library for WebSockets, you can use its 【42†redis adapter†github.com】.\nL308: In this Redis-based architecture, each Cloud Run instance establishes a long-running connection to the Redis channel that contains the received messages (using the 【43†`SUBSCRIBE`†redis.io】 command). Once the container instances receive a new message on the channel, they can send it to their clients over WebSockets in real-time.\nL309: Similarly, when a client emits a message using WebSockets, the instance that receives the message publishes the message to the Redis channel (using the 【44†`PUBLISH`†redis.io】 command), and other instances that are subscribed to this channel will receive this message.\nL310: \nL311: If you want a full code walkthrough, additional code samples are available in the topic 【30†Building a WebSocket Chat service for Cloud Run tutorial】.\nL312: \nL313: [Button: Send feedback ]\nL314: Except as otherwise noted, the content of this page is licensed under the 【45†Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License†creativecommons.org】, and code samples are licensed under the 【46†Apache 2.0 License†www.apache.org】. No send-chat or subscribe control route is publicly exposed.\n\n| Configuration | Requirement |\n| --- | --- |\n| `TWITCH_CLIENT_ID` | Public application ID `6ggythtvgo572dxu8jo4xoaqtn37ix`; not a secret. |\n| `TWITCH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Registered application's secret, operator-provided and available for parent binding as a named Secret Manager environment variable. Never log or commit it. |\n| `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` | Canonical base64 of exactly 32 cryptographically random bytes for AES-256-GCM; identical across instances. A placeholder/password is invalid. Key loss prevents decryption; rotation/migration is not implemented. |\n| `TWITCH_EVENTSUB_SECRET` | Random ASCII webhook HMAC secret, 10–100 characters, shared with subscription transport. Separate from OAuth client secret and encryption key. |\n| `TWITCH_STREAMER_ID`, `TWITCH_BOT_ID` | Distinct numeric Twitch user IDs. Returned token identity must match the configured role's account. This increment supports one streamer and one bot. |\n| `OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI` | Exact registered callback URL ending canonical `/auth/callback` or legacy `/oauth/callback`; no query, fragment, or userinfo. HTTPS required except explicit development `http://localhost`. |\n| `OAUTH_REDIRECT_ALLOWLIST` | Comma-separated exact URLs. Must include the configured canonical URI. No request-controlled redirect is accepted. |\n| `EVENTSUB_CALLBACK_URL` | Owned HTTPS URL ending `/eventsub`, with no query, fragment, or userinfo. Required for subscription creation and production startup. |\n\n**Exact configured callback only:** canonical `/auth/callback` and legacy `/oauth/callback` are supported configuration choices. Only the path in `OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI` is handled; the other returns 404 and cannot consume OAuth state. Authorization and exchange both use that exact allowlisted URI. Configure/register `http://localhost:5191/auth/callback` for an authorized local login or the final `https://<owned-host>/auth/callback` for the first deployment. Legacy clients can keep their exactly registered `/oauth/callback` URI. Do not treat either example as a verified final registration.\n\nThe operator reports secrets are available for the parent to bind through named Secret Manager environment variables (`TWITCH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `TWITCH_EVENTSUB_SECRET`). Codex has not read, received, printed or verified their values. No auth or secret files were read. Secret availability is not a connected OAuth grant: actual streamer/bot authorization remains separate.\n\n`GET /oauth/streamer/start` requests `channel:bot channel:manage:raids`. The raid grant is included now for the owner-committed Raid Send Off feature so consent need not be redone when it is implemented; Send Off itself is still pending. `GET /oauth/bot/start` requests `user:read:chat user:write:chat user:bot`. The bot/chat grants support the selected webhook design without relying on bot moderator status. Validation requires both streamer grants; an older chat-only grant must reconnect. The configured callback exchanges the code using the exact configured redirect, validates client ID, account, scopes and positive expiry, then stores only encrypted access/refresh tokens. Callback errors are generic and never echo provider error descriptions, authorization codes, client secrets, or tokens. The application has no token/request logging; infrastructure request-log redaction still needs review before any live callback URLs are used.\n\nState and browser secrets use 32 random bytes each. Five-minute state records contain only hashes, role and expiry. The state is consumed atomically with a matching browser hash; valid denial/code-error callbacks consume it too. Replay, expiry, cookie duplication, wrong browser, duplicate query parameters, wrong role/account, and unknown callback parameters fail closed. The browser cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/; HTTPS uses Secure and the `__Host-` prefix. It is cleared after callback. Starting another flow in the same browser replaces the cookie; complete one connection at a time.\n\nAES-GCM uses a fresh 96-bit IV and authenticated client/role/account context. Altered ciphertext and cross-role token substitution fail decryption. `oauth.accessToken(role)` validates before every use and refreshes only after validation 401, or an explicit retry after a Helix 401. New refresh tokens are encrypted and saved only after validation. A shared-store 30-second lease serializes refresh/save operations and rejects expired writers; contention fails with a retryable busy error rather than running parallel refreshes. The default HTTP transport has an eight-second per-request timeout, rejects redirects, and redacts transport errors. Network failures after Twitch rotates a token but before storage commits can require reconnecting the account; there is no distributed transaction with Twitch.\n\n## Bot and EventSub\n\n`createRuntime(env, { transport, firestoreClient })` returns the HTTP handler plus OAuth/bot/store services. Dependencies are injected in tests. `runtime.bot.sendChat(message)` is an internal trusted service method; it sends to the configured streamer with the configured bot's validated user token and sender ID. It limits messages to 500 Unicode code points, retries a 401 once after refresh, and treats dropped messages/errors as failures. It does not automatically reply to events. This user-token path can send to all channels in a Twitch Shared Chat session; a source-only app-token sending path is not implemented.\n\n`runtime.bot.chatSubscription()` builds the webhook `channel.chat.message` version 1 payload. `runtime.bot.subscribeChat()` validates both prior grants, obtains an app token using client credentials and submits that payload. These methods make live requests only when called; neither startup nor tests invoke live services. No public control endpoint, automatic subscription provisioning, reconciliation, or raid-subscription registration is included. Do not call them against Twitch until separately authorized.\n\n`POST /eventsub` verifies HMAC-SHA256 over ID + original timestamp + exact raw bytes with a timing-safe digest comparison before parsing. It caps bodies at 64 KiB and rejects malformed JSON/UTF-8, invalid signatures, stale (>10 minutes), future timestamps and invalid consumed schemas. Verified challenges return HTTP 200 raw text with Content-Length equal to the UTF-8 byte length. HTTP 204 acknowledgements omit body, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. Duplicates do not repeat mutations.\n\nRaid notifications create a **local 90-second ritual starting at verified receipt processing**, never synchronized with Twitch. Chat notifications require the configured streamer/bot subscription condition and matching host/event schema. Ordinary chat atomically stores only the latest bounded receipt metadata per host (message/chatter IDs and receipt time), not raw chat text. Recognized marks commands instead use the private marks engine below; mark submissions retain only their normalized text privately for moderation. A signed chat event alone is not proof that a chatter arrived in the raid. There is still no claim endpoint: future claims must require participation from **both incoming raiders and host chat**, with membership/proof rules still to be designed. Revocations are acknowledged/deduplicated; subscription lifecycle and grant deletion are pending.\n\n## Must milestone: marks backend and original runes\n\nThe marks milestone added the backend engine/store integration. The next overlay increment adds a read-only public snapshot and WebSocket below; there are still no public mark mutation, moderation or pending-text endpoints. All service methods are internal trusted interfaces; do not expose them to request-supplied actor objects.\n\n**Fail-closed context:** `app.marks.setKeeperContext(hostId, { streamId, keeperId, optedIn, holdsRelic, blockedUserIds })` requires an explicit authoritative session ID, numeric Keeper ID, boolean consent/ownership, and a bounded configured blocked-user list. Acceptance requires that the Keeper ID equals the signed chat broadcaster, consent is true and the Keeper holds the relic. Only a trusted lifecycle/ownership integration may call this method. Tests inject synthetic trusted contexts; live stream lifecycle and ownership/opt-in synchronization are **not wired yet**. Runtime startup supplies no context, so real marks remain disabled. No ID is inferred from dates, raid events, names or viewer text. Updating the same active stream ID preserves viewer quotas. Selecting a new authoritative stream closes the previous session and removes its viewer quota identifiers; closed stream IDs cannot be reactivated to obtain fresh budgets. Cooldowns survive that transition until their original 30-second expiry.\n\n`!mark word` or `!mark emoji` submits a mark through the already authenticated `channel.chat.message` boundary. Inputs receive Unicode NFKC, locale-independent lowercase and explicit sharp-S/final-sigma folding. The bounded conservative policy accepts one letters/combining-marks word or one supported emoji grapheme (including ZWJ families, modifiers, flags and keycaps). It rejects spaces, control/bidi/invisible word characters, HTML/link syntax and a small substring blocklist. Input is capped at 128 UTF-8 bytes and 32 normalized code points. The filter is intentionally conservative, can reject benign text, and is not comprehensive multilingual abuse/confusable moderation; moderator approval is still required.\n"
      }
    }
  ]
}
